title: Finishing a tractate
hook: a celebration when a tractate is completed

segments.voice: Yesterday, still arguing: Hillel's and Shammai's houses kept disagreeing and kept marrying each other. Today, what happens when a book is finished.

The last line of a tractate. Someone reads it aloud, slowly, and the room that has been quiet for an hour suddenly isn't. A cake appears from somewhere. Someone pours a drink. Someone else stands up to say a few words about the final page, gets interrupted, and starts again. Months of study, sometimes years, one page at a time, and now the book is closed. It is not a quiet moment. It's a party. Today's word is the name of that party.
screen: `THE LAST LINE, READ ALOUD.` → `A CAKE APPEARS.` → `A BOOK CLOSES. A PARTY STARTS.`

segments.voice: Siyum. Completion, and the celebration that marks it. First, an old feast. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, tells of the sage Abaye saying that whenever he saw a young scholar finish a tractate, he made a feast for the rabbis. Notice whose finish it was. Not his own. He threw the party for somebody else's last page. Second, what's said. At a siyum, those who finished say a short traditional text called the hadran. It speaks to the tractate itself, by name, as if to a friend: we will return to you, and you will return to us. We won't forget you, and you won't forget us. The ending isn't goodbye; it's see you again. Third, the meal. The meal after a siyum is treated as a seudat mitzvah, a meal that is itself part of a commandment, like the meal at a wedding or a circumcision. A custom grows out of that. On the day before Passover, by custom, firstborns fast. Some attend a siyum that morning, and joining its meal releases them from the fast. Fourth, the size. A siyum can be three people around a kitchen table who finished a small tractate together, or a crowd in a large hall when a daily study cycle reaches the end of the whole Talmud. Same words, same promise to return.
screen: `ABAYE'S FEAST FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · `WE WILL RETURN TO YOU.` · `A MEAL THAT IS A COMMANDMENT.` · `A KITCHEN TABLE OR A GREAT HALL.` · then, large: `THE SIYUM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you finished recently, a project, a book, a hard week, a course of treatment, and let yourself see its last page. Don't judge how well it went; a siyum marks reaching the end, not doing it perfectly. Then tell it, quietly, what the hadran tells a tractate: I'll come back to you.
Siyum. Completion: the celebration when a tractate, or another unit of study, is finished, with the hadran's promise to return. Today's word.
Your line: the siyum. Someone else's finish is worth a feast too. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: When a person or group completes a tractate, they hold a siyum: the last passage is read, the hadran is recited, someone teaches a few words on the tractate, and a festive meal follows. A siyum is often held on the morning before Passover so that firstborns may join the meal.

chat.says: Why does a Talmud class throw a party at the end of a book?
options: It's a siyum: finishing is celebrated, with a promise to return to the book.
It's to say goodbye to the book for good, since it's finished and done.
It's only a modern habit; the Talmud itself never mentions a feast for finishing.
